value.title: Intentional Action and Side-Effects in Ordinary Language

participants.population: People spending time in a Manhattan public park.

Experiment 1.population: People spending time in a Manhattan public park.

Experiment 2.population: People spending time in a Manhattan public park.

steps: Participants are randomly assigned to either a 'harm condition' or a 'help condition'.
Participants read a vignette (either about a corporate chairman or a military lieutenant) implementing a plan with a known side-effect that the agent claims not to care about.
Participants assess how much blame (in the harm condition) or praise (in the help condition) the agent deserves on a scale from 0 to 6.
Participants answer a categorical (Yes/No) question regarding whether the agent brought about the side-effect intentionally.

value.title: Intentional Action and Side-Effects in Ordinary Language

findings.main_hypothesis: A person’s intuitions as to whether or not a given side-effect was produced 'intentionally' can be influenced by that person’s attitude toward the specific side-effect in question (specifically whether it is good or bad).

statistical_tests.statistical_hypothesis: Intentionality judgments differ between harm and help conditions.

original_data_points.description: Percentage of participants judging the side-effect as intentional.

findings.main_hypothesis: People are considerably more willing to blame the agent for bad side-effects than to praise the agent for good side-effects.

statistical_tests.statistical_hypothesis: Mean blame in harm condition > Mean praise in help condition.

original_data_points.description: Mean praise/blame scores on a 0-6 scale.

findings.main_hypothesis: The effect observed in Experiment 1 is general and not specific to corporations or environmental damage.

statistical_tests.statistical_hypothesis: Intentionality judgments differ between harm and help conditions in a military context.

original_data_points.description: Percentage of participants judging the side-effect as intentional.

findings.main_hypothesis: The asymmetry in praise and blame assignment may be at the root of the asymmetry in the application of the concept intentional.

statistical_tests.statistical_hypothesis: Praise/blame scores are correlated with intentionality judgments.

original_data_points.description: Correlation between moral judgment and intentionality judgment across both experiments.

overall_original_results.description: Summary of intentionality judgments and moral evaluations across two experiments.

value.title: Thinking through Uncertainty: Nonconsequential Reasoning and Choice

steps: Subjects played a series of 40 one-shot games, including Prisoner's Dilemma (PD) games against different opponents.
PD games were presented in triads consisting of three versions: opponent strategy unknown, opponent known to have competed, and opponent known to have cooperated.
PD games were interspersed with other two-person games to prevent the development of standard strategies.
Subjects participated in a version of Newcomb's problem involving two boxes (A and B) and a computer program that predicted their choice with 92% success.
Subjects chose between taking both Box A and Box B or taking only Box B.
A separate group of subjects played PD games and were offered the opportunity to pay a small fee to learn the opponent's decision before making their own choice.

value.title: Thinking through Uncertainty: Nonconsequential Reasoning and Choice

findings.main_hypothesis: People exhibit a greater rate of cooperation in the disjunctive condition (when the other player's strategy is not known) than when the other player's strategy is known to be either 'compete' or 'cooperate'.

statistical_tests.statistical_hypothesis: Cooperation Rate (Unknown) ≠ Cooperation Rate (Known Cooperate) ≠ Cooperation Rate (Known Compete)
Frequency of Disjunction Pattern (Compete if Known, Cooperate if Unknown) > 0

original_data_points.description: Cooperation rates across 444 triads of Prisoner's Dilemma games played by 80 subjects.

findings.main_hypothesis: A majority of subjects will choose a single box (Box B) in a version of Newcomb's problem that lacks supernatural elements, despite the dominance of taking both boxes.

original_data_points.description: Choices in a computer-simulated Newcomb's Problem.

findings.main_hypothesis: People will pay to obtain information that they do not use to change their decision, seeking it to clarify reasons rather than to inform choice.

statistical_tests.statistical_hypothesis: Percentage of subjects paying for information > 0%

original_data_points.description: Information seeking behavior and subsequent choice in PD games.

Choice after seeing information.observation: Great majority chose to compete regardless of opponent's decision

overall_original_results.description: A comprehensive repository of numerical findings from the PD triads, Newcomb's problem, and information-seeking tasks.

value.title: Testing the decoy effect to improve online survey participation: Evidence from a field experiment

preliminary_questionnaire.details: 241 individuals clicked the survey link and started the preliminary questionnaire; 216 completed the questionnaire; 210 provided an email address to be invited to the experiment. Recruited in August 2022 from students registered at a UK-based university through Facebook, WhatsApp, and WeChat.

main_experiment.details: 210 invitation emails sent; 7 emails bounced (4 from control, 3 from decoy), leaving 203 who received the experimental invitation. Randomized in Microsoft Excel. Sample characteristics among the 203 valid-email participants: age 20-24: 55 (27.1%), 25-29: 102 (50.2%), 30-35: 46 (22.7%); male: 106 (52.2%), female: 97 (47.8%); White: 117 (57.6%), Asian: 48 (23.7%), Black: 34 (16.7%), Other: 4 (2.0%); Christian: 146 (71.9%), Other religion: 18 (8.9%), No religion: 39 (19.2%); Bachelor's degree: 105 (51.7%), Graduate/professional degree: 98 (48.3%).

control_group.description: Received email invitation with only the target survey option

decoy_group.description: Received email invitation with both target and decoy survey options

decoy_target_first.description: Decoy group randomized to see target survey first in the comparison table

decoy_decoy_first.description: Decoy group randomized to see decoy survey first in the comparison table

design.type: between-subjects field experiment with nested randomization of option order within the decoy condition
design.secondary_factor: Presentation order within decoy condition (target first vs decoy first)

conditions.name: Control
conditions.description: Email invitation offers only the target survey (Fear of Coronavirus Questionnaire with 8 closed-ended questions; £2 Amazon voucher after 1 week)

conditions.name: Decoy - Target First
conditions.description: Email invitation offers both target (closed-ended, £2 after 1 week) and decoy (open-ended, £2 after 4 weeks) surveys in table format with target shown first

conditions.name: Decoy - Decoy First
conditions.description: Email invitation offers both target (closed-ended, £2 after 1 week) and decoy (open-ended, £2 after 4 weeks) surveys in table format with decoy shown first

procedure.name: Preliminary questionnaire recruitment
procedure.details: Students at a UK-based university were contacted via social media (Facebook, WhatsApp, WeChat) with a survey on fear of coronavirus. Participants completed a preliminary questionnaire assessing attitudes toward question type (close-ended vs open-ended) and payment delay (1 week vs 4 weeks) and provided demographics. At the end, participants could provide their email address for an Amazon voucher of £2 to participate in the main survey.

procedure.name: Main field experiment
procedure.details: Individuals who had provided email addresses were sent an email invitation to the main questionnaire. Participants were randomized in Microsoft Excel into control or decoy conditions. Within the decoy condition, participants were further randomized with equal probability to one of two presentation orders: target first or decoy first. No reminder emails were sent.

procedure.name: Target survey completion (if selected)
procedure.details: Target survey consisted of: (1) Demographics (4 items); (2) Fear of Coronavirus Questionnaire (8 items, 1-5 Likert scale); (3) Debrief questions (2-3 items depending on condition). Reward: £2 Amazon voucher after 1 week.

procedure.name: Decoy survey completion (if selected in decoy condition)
procedure.details: Decoy survey consisted of: (1) Demographics (4 items); (2) Two open-ended questions requiring minimum 100 words each on coronavirus attitudes and precautions; (3) Debrief questions (4-5 items). Reward: £2 Amazon voucher after 4 weeks (stated reason: responses need to be coded).

Perceived influence of decoy on decision
secondary_outcomes.unit_of_analysis: Per target completer in decoy condition

dependent_variables: Demographic composition of completers vs non-completers (secondary)

value.title: Testing the decoy effect to improve online survey participation: Evidence from a field experiment

preliminary_study_findings.description: Respondents generally preferred close-ended questions over open-ended questions.
preliminary_study_findings.hypothesis: Open-ended questions would be perceived as less attractive than close-ended questions and therefore could function as an inferior decoy attribute.
preliminary_study_findings.raw_outcomes: Among N=210 preliminary questionnaire respondents: close-ended questions 61.4% (n~129), open-ended questions 7.9% (n~17), indifferent 30.7% (n~64). Exact counts NOT PROVIDED in paper.

preliminary_study_findings.description: Most respondents indicated they would not participate if remuneration were received only after four weeks.
preliminary_study_findings.hypothesis: Delayed remuneration would be perceived as less attractive than sooner remuneration and therefore could function as an inferior decoy attribute.
preliminary_study_findings.raw_outcomes: Among N=210 preliminary questionnaire respondents: Definitely not 1.0% (n~2), Probably not 85.1% (n~179), Probably yes 1.5% (n~3), Definitely yes 12.4% (n~26). Overall 86.1% would not respond if remuneration in four weeks.

main_study.study_name: Field experiment on the decoy effect in survey participation

findings.description: Randomization produced similar groups on most sociodemographic variables, except ethnicity.
findings.hypothesis: No explicit hypothesis; balance checks were used to compare control and decoy groups.

statistical_tests.claim: No age difference between control and decoy groups.
No gender difference between control and decoy groups.
Ethnicity differed between conditions; the decoy condition contained more White participants (67.7% vs 47.5%).
No religion difference between control and decoy groups at conventional significance levels.
No education difference between control and decoy groups.

findings.description: The presence of the decoy option increased completion of the target survey.
findings.hypothesis: Among those likely to take part in a survey, the presence of a decoy version of the same survey on the invitation will increase the chances of completing the target version.

raw_data.note: Table 2 / Table S3 reports decoy as 59.8%, but text, flow diagram, and participant-level data imply 57/102 = 55.9%

findings.description: Most target-survey completers in the decoy condition reported that the decoy had at least somewhat influenced their decision to participate.
findings.hypothesis: The decoy option should be perceived as influencing participation decisions.
findings.raw_outcomes: Among the 57 individuals in the decoy condition who completed the target survey, 33/57 (57.9%) at least somewhat agreed that the decoy survey had influenced their decision to participate.

findings.description: There was little evidence for adverse question-response behavior or non-response bias, except for ethnicity differences.
findings.hypothesis: The decoy should increase participation without negatively influencing question response behavior or inducing substantial non-response bias.
